key_facts: Divergence measures how the vector field behaves towards or away from a point.
It quantifies the 'outflowing-neness' of a vector field in R2 or R3.
Fields with zero divergence do not have net flow in or out, representing source-free fields.
A vector field with positive divergence indicates flow away from a point.
The divergence of a vector field F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ in R^3 is div F = Px + Qy + Rz.
misconceptions: Some students confuse divergence with curl, thinking both measure the same aspect of vector fields.
A misconception among students is that a non-zero divergence implies the vector field has no practical applications.
canonical_examples: Vector field F(x,y) = ⟨x^2 y, y - xy^2⟩ has a divergence of 1, indicating it is not source-free.
Vector field F(x,y) = ⟨-y, x⟩ has a divergence of 0, indicating it is source-free.
Vector field F(x,y) = ⟨-y, x⟩ has a divergence of 0 everywhere, representing no net flow.
Vector field F(x,y) = ⟨-yx, x^2⟩ has a divergence of -y, indicating it concentrates towards the positive y-axis and disperses from the negative y-axis.
